pft10_triple_bottleneck.description: PFT#10 fine root underestimation caused by three simultaneous bottlenecks: catastrophic P starvation (uptake/demand ≈ 0.000005), strong light competition from PFT#9 (5-10× GPP advantage), and excessive fine root turnover rate (1 year vs 5 year realistic)
pft10_triple_bottleneck.mechanism: P starvation prevents biomass production → small leaf area loses light competition → low GPP reduces C for growth → less root growth reduces P uptake → positive feedback loop. Turnover rate controls steady-state biomass = allocation/turnover

pid_controller_paradox.description: Responsive allocation (high pid_kp) performs worse than locked allocation (low pid_kp) when PID responds to wrong stress signal
pid_controller_paradox.mechanism: When total productivity extremely low, PID detects light limitation as dominant signal rather than P stress. Increases target L2FR from 0.972 to 2.040 (more leaf allocation), but without P cannot produce leaf biomass, causing total biomass collapse

turnover_first_order_control.description: Fine root turnover rate is first-order control on standing biomass, more important than allocation rate
turnover_first_order_control.mechanism: Steady-state biomass = Allocation rate / Turnover rate. Test2 had lowest allocation (27.28 g C/m²/yr) but highest biomass (120.48 g C/m²) due to 5× lower turnover rate

morris_ensemble_missing_critical_params.description: fates_turnover_fnrt was NOT included in the 138-parameter Morris ensemble, causing systematic bias in ALL 4329 simulation cases
morris_ensemble_missing_critical_params.mechanism: All simulations used same turnover rate (1.0 year for PFT#10) which is 5× too fast compared to literature values. Morris optimization could not discover this bottleneck because parameter was not varied

extremely_low_p_uptake_despite_morris_pa.description: P uptake parameters (vmax_p, vmax_ptase, alpha_ptase) ARE in Morris ensemble, yet ALL cases show extremely low P uptake (uptake/demand ≈ 0.000005), indicating severe P limitation that Morris ranges cannot overcome
extremely_low_p_uptake_despite_morris_pa.mechanism: Even with P uptake parameters in optimization space, PFT#10 P uptake/demand ratio ≈ 5 parts per million across all cases. This is NOT zero but extremely small. Possible causes: Morris ranges too narrow, soil P depletion, PFT competition, or catch-22 (need roots to get P, need P to grow roots)

zero_overlap_parameter_trade_offs.description: Method 1 (graminoid-focused) and Method 2 (multi-PFT balanced) parameter sets have 0% overlap, revealing fundamental antagonistic parameter effects between PFTs
zero_overlap_parameter_trade_offs.mechanism: Parameters that increase PFT#10 (graminoid) fineroot biomass suppress PFT#9 (deciduous shrub) performance, creating competitive exclusion rather than coexistence

multi_pft_optimization_impossibility.description: Essentially zero Morris simulations (0.00-0.07%) achieve realistic biomass for all 3 Arctic PFTs simultaneously
multi_pft_optimization_impossibility.mechanism: Current parameter space is inadequate for realistic multi-PFT Arctic ecosystems due to parameter trade-offs and competitive exclusion

pft_specific_parameter_independence.description: PFT-specific parameters allow independent optimization without affecting other PFTs
pft_specific_parameter_independence.mechanism: Parameters with _9 suffix only affect PFT#9 mortality, allocation, and recruitment, leaving PFT#7 and PFT#10 performance unchanged

set_3930_optimal_baseline.description: Set #3930 achieves perfect PFT#7 and PFT#9 performance (6/6 outputs) with only PFT#10 needing improvement
set_3930_optimal_baseline.mechanism: Provides ideal baseline for hybrid parameter modification since shrub communities are already realistic

parameter_bounds_limitations.description: 29/138 parameters (21%) are at Morris sampling bounds in Set #3643, suggesting optimal parameters lie outside current bounds
parameter_bounds_limitations.mechanism: Morris sampling bounds may be too restrictive, limiting exploration of parameter space

cross_pft_competition_pervasive.description: Parameters from one PFT frequently rank in top 5 for other PFTs, with 20-40% of top-10 parameters being cross-PFT effects
cross_pft_competition_pervasive.mechanism: Competition for light (crown area) and nutrients (uptake kinetics) create indirect effects where one PFT's parameters directly affect another PFT's biomass

pft9_crown_suppresses_pft10.description: PFT#9 crown area parameter is 2nd most important for PFT#10 fineroot biomass with strong negative effect (μ=-17.7)
pft9_crown_suppresses_pft10.mechanism: Larger PFT#9 crowns shade graminoids, reducing photosynthesis and subsequently root growth

phosphatase_counterintuitive_negative.description: Alpha_ptase_7 has NEGATIVE effect on leaf biomass (μ=-73.5) despite increasing P availability
phosphatase_counterintuitive_negative.mechanism: Higher phosphatase activity may involve C costs of enzyme production, P-induced allocation shifts, or P mineralization favoring competitors

pid_controller_dysfunction_pft10.description: PID gain has NEGATIVE effect on BOTH leaf and fineroot biomass for PFT#10, opposite of expected behavior
pid_controller_dysfunction_pft10.mechanism: Over-allocation to roots causes C starvation and mortality, or PID oscillation reduces efficiency

storage_cushion_pft_specific_effects.description: Storage cushion has opposite effects across PFTs: POSITIVE for PFT#7 and #10, NEGATIVE for PFT#9 leaf
storage_cushion_pft_specific_effects.mechanism: Arctic graminoids depend on C storage for winter survival, deciduous shrubs trade off storage vs growth

phenology_shared_parameter_tradeoffs.description: Shared phenology parameters have opposite effects: POSITIVE for PFT#7, NEGATIVE for PFT#9/10
phenology_shared_parameter_tradeoffs.mechanism: Evergreen benefits from higher GDD thresholds while deciduous suffers from later leaf-out and shorter season

reproduction_dominates_pft9.description: Reproduction parameters (seed supplement, N fixation) dominate PFT#9 biomass, not phenology as previously thought
reproduction_dominates_pft9.mechanism: More seed supplement increases establishment leading to more individuals and total biomass

exponential_phenology_sensitivity.description: Phenology parameters in exponential functions create extreme sensitivity - small changes in phen_c cause large timing changes due to exponential amplification
exponential_phenology_sensitivity.mechanism: GDD_threshold = phen_a + phen_b × exp(phen_c × nchilldays). At 165 chilling days, small phen_c change (0.00361) gets amplified by exp function then multiplied by large phen_b (638), causing 52-day timing shift

arctic_winter_chilling_collapse.description: Arctic winter accumulates ~165 chilling days, causing GDD threshold to collapse to near-zero (~0.5°C-days), triggering premature leaf-on
arctic_winter_chilling_collapse.mechanism: High chilling days drive exponential term toward zero: exp(-0.01352 × 165) = 0.107, making threshold = -68 + 638 × 0.107 ≈ 0.5°C-days

morris_grid_resolution_limitation.description: Morris sampling with num_levels=8 creates discrete grid that can miss optimal parameter values falling between grid points
morris_grid_resolution_limitation.mechanism: Optimized phen_c = -0.00991 falls between Morris grid Level 3 (-0.01074) and Level 4 (-0.00935), explaining why 4,170 parameter combinations showed poor phenology

phenology_magnitude_separation.description: Phenology parameters control WHEN leaves appear but not HOW MUCH leaf area develops - timing and magnitude are controlled by different parameter sets
phenology_magnitude_separation.mechanism: Phenology parameters (phen_c, phen_chilltemp) control leaf-on date. LAI magnitude controlled by allocation parameters (alloc_storage_cushion, leaf_slatop, pid_kp, allometry)

initialization_artifacts.description: First 2 years (2000-2001) of phenology simulation have artifacts because PyModel starts with nchilldays=0 instead of ~165 from previous fall
initialization_artifacts.mechanism: Model initialization doesn't account for chilling accumulation from fall 1999, causing wrong GDD threshold calculation in first two years

negative_npp_during_observed_growth.description: FATES simulates negative NPP (-0.05 g C/m²/day) during DOY 100-140 when MODIS observations show real plants successfully growing (starting DOY 127)
negative_npp_during_observed_growth.mechanism: Maintenance respiration (0.08 g C/m²/day) exceeds extremely low GPP (0.03 g C/m²/day) in early spring, creating carbon deficit when real plants are building leaf area

spring_carbon_starvation_mechanism.description: Case #3643 shows spring carbon starvation (MR > GPP during DOY 100-140) preventing LAI growth despite optimized parameters
spring_carbon_starvation_mechanism.mechanism: Even with maintresp_nonleaf_baserate at lower bound (1.296e-6), spring MR (0.05 g C/m²/day) exceeds spring GPP (0.03 g C/m²/day), creating cumulative deficit of -0.73 g C/m² by DOY 127

allocation_logic_prevents_storage_invest.description: FATES allocation framework requires positive NPP before growth allocation, preventing storage-investment strategy that real Arctic plants use
allocation_logic_prevents_storage_invest.mechanism: Real plants invest stored C to build initial leaves → more leaves increase GPP → creates positive NPP → enables continued growth. FATES cannot do this because allocation requires positive NPP first

maintenance_respiration_still_excessive_.description: Even with 49% reduced maintenance respiration baserate (1.296e-6), maintenance costs still exceed GPP in early spring
maintenance_respiration_still_excessive_.mechanism: Fine-roots maintained year-round create continuous cost that exceeds very low spring photosynthesis, unlike temperate deciduous trees that shed leaves in winter

parameter_space_exhaustion.description: 21% of parameters (29 out of 138) are at their Morris sampling bounds, preventing further optimization of carbon balance despite already-optimized phenology and stoichiometry
parameter_space_exhaustion.mechanism: Critical parameters for carbon balance (maintresp_nonleaf_baserate at lower bound, leaf_slatop_10 at lower bound) cannot be adjusted further within Morris parameter space to fix spring carbon starvation (MR 0.05 > GPP 0.03 g C/m²/day)

phenology_already_solved.description: Case #3643 has phenology parameters very close to Dec 7 optimized values (phen_chilltemp 2.256°C vs optimized 2.262°C), indicating phenology timing is not the constraint
phenology_already_solved.mechanism: Case #3643 is from phenology-calibrated Morris sets with already-optimized phenology parameters, achieving RMSE 4.2 days. The 13-day early cold status (DOY 114 vs MODIS 127) is acceptable given model structure

carbon_starvation_prevents_growth.description: Spring carbon deficit (-0.73 g C/m² by DOY 127) prevents LAI growth allocation despite correct phenology timing and optimized stoichiometry
carbon_starvation_prevents_growth.mechanism: Spring maintenance respiration (0.05 g C/m²/day) exceeds GPP (0.03 g C/m²/day) during DOY 100-140, creating cumulative carbon deficit that prevents positive NPP needed for growth allocation until DOY 195

fates_mr_has_q10_adjustment.description: FATES already implements Q10 temperature adjustment for maintenance respiration, but uses inappropriate 20°C reference temperature for Arctic
fates_mr_has_q10_adjustment.mechanism: Current formula: MR(T) = baserate × Q10^((T - 20°C) / 10°C). At Arctic spring temperatures (5°C), this gives 65-72% reduction from 20°C baseline, but still produces MR > GPP

dormancy_mr_suppression_missing.description: FATES continues normal MR calculation even when elong_factor = 0 (dormant state), but real Arctic plants have minimal survival metabolism during dormancy
dormancy_mr_suppression_missing.mechanism: Arctic plants enter physiological dormancy in winter with MR reduced to 10-20% of active levels. FATES lacks this dormancy-dependent MR suppression mechanism

opposite_bounds_competitive_signal.description: Parameters hitting opposite bounds across PFTs indicate competitive niche differentiation rather than random optimization
opposite_bounds_competitive_signal.mechanism: Same parameters at lower bound for one PFT but upper bound for another PFT reveals evolutionary trade-offs and competitive dynamics under nutrient limitation

fates_life_history_guilds.description: FATES code explicitly recognizes four functional guilds: short-lived pioneers, long-lived pioneers, partial-shade-tolerants, and shade-tolerants
fates_life_history_guilds.mechanism: Code references Poorter et al. work and implements photoblastic germination and seed bank strategies that differentiate r/K selection strategies

nh4_uptake_niche_differentiation.description: 5 orders of magnitude difference in NH4 uptake capacity between PFTs represents extreme niche specialization
nh4_uptake_niche_differentiation.mechanism: PFT#9 uses aggressive NH4 acquisition strategy while PFT#10 uses conservative strategy focusing on P acquisition and N retranslocation

mortality_coexistence_mechanism.description: High background mortality for dominant PFT prevents competitive exclusion of subordinate PFTs
mortality_coexistence_mechanism.mechanism: Evergreen shrubs have 2.87x higher mortality than other PFTs, creating recruitment opportunities through gap dynamics (Janzen-Connell effect)

seed_bank_temporal_partitioning.description: Opposite seed decay rates create temporal niche differentiation through persistent vs transient seed banks
seed_bank_temporal_partitioning.mechanism: Evergreen shrubs maintain persistent seed banks (3.7 yr residence) while herbaceous PFTs use transient seed banks (1.4 yr residence) for rapid gap exploitation

mr_reduction_ecosystem_collapse.description: Reducing maintenance respiration by 90% triggers catastrophic ecosystem collapse over 20-year timescale
mr_reduction_ecosystem_collapse.mechanism: Lower MR → Less tissue maintenance → Faster biomass loss → Lower GPP → Less carbon for growth → Death spiral feedback loop

storage_cushion_baseline_dependency.description: Storage cushion effect reverses sign depending on baseline ecosystem health
storage_cushion_baseline_dependency.mechanism: From collapsed ecosystem: Extra C wasted on roots. From healthy ecosystem: Extra C available for growth

pid_gain_graminoid_allocation.description: Reducing PID gain by 50% consistently improves PFT#10 (graminoid) leaf biomass by 30-58%
pid_gain_graminoid_allocation.mechanism: Lower PID gain → Less aggressive root allocation → More carbon available for leaves

allocation_hierarchy_problem.description: Spring carbon allocation follows Storage refill → Root turnover replacement → NEW leaf growth order, causing insufficient spring LAI buildup
allocation_hierarchy_problem.mechanism: By the time allocation reaches leaf growth, spring growing season is half over and carbon is depleted

storage_priority_no_annual_effect.description: Storage priority parameter has no effect on annual mean biomass values across multiple test series
storage_priority_no_annual_effect.mechanism: May affect intra-annual timing/dynamics but not annual averages

arctic_graminoid_unique_allocation.description: PFT#10 (Arctic Graminoid) has fundamentally different biomass allocation than shrubs, with 5.5× higher fineroot:leaf ratio
arctic_graminoid_unique_allocation.mechanism: Graminoids allocate much more carbon to belowground structures, requiring very different parameter values than shrubs

phenology_biomass_decoupling.description: Parameters controlling seasonal timing are independent from those controlling biomass allocation
phenology_biomass_decoupling.mechanism: Phenology parameters are SHARED across PFTs while allocation parameters are PFT-specific, allowing independent optimization

morris_ensemble_equifinality.description: Multiple parameter combinations achieve similar biomass performance despite vastly different underlying parameter values
morris_ensemble_equifinality.mechanism: Top 50 sets show 2-8× variation in parameter values while maintaining similar composite NRMSE scores

multi_output_optimization_difficulty.description: Only 1.15% of Morris ensemble (48/4170) satisfies all 6 biomass targets simultaneously
multi_output_optimization_difficulty.mechanism: Conflicting requirements between PFT biomass targets make simultaneous optimization extremely challenging

parameter_modifications_case_specific.description: Parameter modifications are NOT universally beneficial - only 54% of cases improve with the best modification strategy, and the original Morris best case actually gets worse with modifications
parameter_modifications_case_specific.mechanism: Different parameter regimes respond differently to the same modifications due to parameter interactions and case-specific optimization states

phenology_calibration_instability.description: Universal phenology parameters calibrated from one case cause 54% failure rate when applied to other parameter combinations
phenology_calibration_instability.mechanism: Phenology parameters calibrated using Case #561 are incompatible with certain Morris parameter combinations, potentially causing premature leaf-out, delayed dormancy, or extreme LAI values leading to simulation crashes

storage_cushion_stabilizes_without_impro.description: Increasing storage cushion from Morris range to 3.0 prevents simulation crashes but doesn't improve performance (68% still regress)
storage_cushion_stabilizes_without_impro.mechanism: Storage cushion provides sufficient carbon buffer to prevent crashes but doesn't address underlying allocation imbalance and may worsen allocation if PID controller allocates excess carbon to storage

pid_reduction_case_dependent.description: Reducing PID gain from ~0.003 to 0.000005 improves 54% of cases but worsens 46%, with performance changes ranging from -21.8% to +33.4%
pid_reduction_case_dependent.mechanism: Low PID gain reduces fineroot over-allocation for cases where PID was driving excessive root growth, but fails for cases where Morris PID value was already appropriate or may be antagonistic to certain allometry/storage parameter combinations

phenology_case_representativeness.description: Phenology parameters calibrated from Case #2675 (best Morris case) eliminate all simulation failures, while those calibrated from Case #561 cause 54% failure rate
phenology_case_representativeness.mechanism: Phenology parameters must be calibrated from representative cases in successful parameter space regions. Case #2675 phenology is universally compatible because it represents parameter combinations that work well for Arctic ecosystems

biomass_lai_gpp_tradeoff.description: Cases optimized for biomass (leaf + fineroot carbon) systematically overestimate MODIS LAI and GPP by 2-3× despite achieving low biomass NRMSE
biomass_lai_gpp_tradeoff.mechanism: Single-objective optimization on biomass creates trade-offs with ecosystem fluxes. Possible mechanisms include lower specific leaf area, higher photosynthetic efficiency, or canopy structure differences

full_modification_effectiveness.description: Combined phenology + storage cushion + PID modifications are most effective, with 60% of top 10 cases using full modification suite (phen2675stc3pid)
full_modification_effectiveness.mechanism: Phenology alone is insufficient - storage buffering and PID allocation adjustments work synergistically to improve multi-PFT performance

multi_pft_validation_challenge.description: NO case achieves all 6 biomass outputs (3 PFTs × 2 pools) within ±20% of observations, with maximum of 3/6 outputs satisfied
multi_pft_validation_challenge.mechanism: Fundamental parameter trade-offs exist between PFTs in the model structure that prevent simultaneous optimization across all plant functional types

parameter_space_constrains_phenology_suc.description: Case #2675 has 30.4% of parameters at bounds vs 21.0% for Case #3643, indicating different parameter regimes require different phenology calibrations
parameter_space_constrains_phenology_suc.mechanism: Parameters at bounds create constraints that affect carbon balance, photosynthesis, and phenology interactions differently across parameter space

opposite_parameter_constraints_between_c.description: Key parameters (maintresp_nonleaf_baserate, leaf_slatop_10) are at opposite bounds between Case #2675 and #3643
opposite_parameter_constraints_between_c.mechanism: Case #2675 has high maintenance respiration and high SLA while Case #3643 has low maintenance respiration and low SLA, creating fundamentally different carbon dynamics

storage_cushion_optimization_potential.description: Case #2675 has alloc_storage_cushion_10 at lower bound (0.686) while Case #3643 is mid-range, providing more room for improvement
storage_cushion_optimization_potential.mechanism: Lower bound position means storage cushion can be increased significantly without parameter space conflicts, enabling better winter survival

biomass_ecosystem_function_tradeoff.description: Optimizing for biomass creates 2-3x overestimation of ecosystem LAI and GPP, while cases that match MODIS ecosystem function severely underestimate individual PFT biomass
biomass_ecosystem_function_tradeoff.mechanism: Biomass-optimized cases require high biomass which combined with high SLA creates excessive LAI, leading to unrealistic GPP. Cases with correct ecosystem function sacrifice PFT#9 through high microbial competition

pft9_parameterization_problem.description: PFT#9 (Cold Deciduous Shrub) parameterization is fundamentally problematic - matching its biomass leads to ecosystem function failure
pft9_parameterization_problem.mechanism: PFT#9 likely has incorrect SLA and tissue properties. High biomass needed to match observations combined with high SLA produces excessive LAI contribution

microbial_competition_controls_pft_domin.description: Opposite microbial biomass strategies control which PFTs dominate - high microbial competition suppresses specific PFTs
microbial_competition_controls_pft_domin.mechanism: Case #845 uses high microb_bio_9 (420) to suppress PFT#9 and low microb_bio_10 (180) to favor PFT#10, opposite strategy from optimized case #2678

phenology_timing_ecosystem_control.description: Shorter growing season through warmer cold temperature threshold reduces peak LAI duration and matches MODIS seasonal patterns
phenology_timing_ecosystem_control.mechanism: Case #845 uses phen_coldtemp = +2.9°C vs #2675 = -7.5°C, creating later leaf-on and shorter growing season that reduces LAI peaks

allocation_paradox.description: Higher P uptake capacity (vmax_p) can cause catastrophic biomass collapse through allocation feedback
allocation_paradox.mechanism: vmax_p increase → higher P uptake per root → higher storage P → C:P ratio decreases → PID controller reduces root allocation → lower total capacitance → less total P uptake → biomass collapse

storage_vs_allocation_paradox.description: Total productivity matters more than allocation ratio for biomass accumulation. Case #845 has higher L:FR (9.88, less fineroot allocation) but produces more absolute fineroot biomass than Case #2678 with lower L:FR (2.37, more fineroot allocation).
storage_vs_allocation_paradox.mechanism: You can't allocate what you don't produce. Higher total productivity from better storage and survival creates more absolute biomass even with lower allocation fractions.

triple_mortality_trap_pft9.description: PFT#9 fails in Case #845 due to simultaneous high C starvation mortality (2.5× higher), lower drought tolerance (2.5× lower threshold), and fast seed decay (2.3× faster), creating a death spiral with no recovery.
triple_mortality_trap_pft9.mechanism: High adult mortality plus low recruitment equals local extinction. Multiple mortality sources compound rather than being independent.

survival_trumps_productivity.description: PFT#9 in Case #845 has higher Vcmax (81.8 vs 58.4) and shorter dormancy (66 vs 121 days) but still fails due to mortality parameters. Dead plants can't photosynthesize.
survival_trumps_productivity.mechanism: Must solve survival first, then optimize growth. High productivity parameters are useless if the plant dies during winter or drought.

growing_season_biomass_tradeoff.description: Cannot simultaneously optimize biomass match and ecosystem LAI/GPP. Long growing season matches biomass but creates 2-3× MODIS overestimate. Short growing season matches MODIS but loses one PFT.
growing_season_biomass_tradeoff.mechanism: Phenology formulation couples growing season length to all PFTs via single phen_coldtemp parameter. Temperature threshold of -7.46°C vs +2.92°C creates fundamentally different ecosystem behavior.

microbial_competition_niche_separation.description: Opposite microbial competition patterns create PFT winners and losers. Case #2678 favors PFT#7 (microb_bio=140) and PFT#9 (300), suppresses PFT#10 (340). Case #845 reverses this pattern.
microbial_competition_niche_separation.mechanism: Microbial competition creates PFT-specific bottlenecks that interact with nutrient uptake strategies. High competition forces high-affinity, low-Vmax strategies.

storage_cushion_critical_threshold.description: alloc_storage_cushion_10 is the #1 Morris parameter for PFT#10 fineroot biomass. Even extreme modifications (0.686 → 3.0, 4.4× increase beyond Morris bounds) still don't fully solve PFT#10 underestimation.
storage_cushion_critical_threshold.mechanism: Arctic plants need large storage for 9-month winter maintenance respiration, early spring growth before photosynthesis, and buffering nutrient limitations. Storage becomes structural tissue over multiple years.

morris_parameter_space_insufficient.description: 4170 Morris simulations produced ZERO cases with all 3 PFTs within uncertainty AND realistic ecosystem LAI/GPP. Top cases represent opposite extremes with no intermediate solutions.
morris_parameter_space_insufficient.mechanism: The parameter space contains only Type A solutions (good biomass, bad LAI) and Type B solutions (good LAI, missing PFT). No Type C solutions exist.

pft9_mortality_trap_mechanism.description: PFT#9 fails due to a triple mortality trap: high C starvation mortality (0.787), low drought tolerance (5.2e-7), and poor recruitment (fast seed decay 0.731, low storage 0.887)
pft9_mortality_trap_mechanism.mechanism: Winter C starvation kills cohorts, summer drought stress kills survivors, fast seed decay prevents recruitment replacement, creating population collapse to near-zero

cumulative_parameter_effects.description: Each parameter modification contributes progressively to PFT#9 improvement: Exp1 (4-8x), Exp2 (+50-100%), Exp3 (+20-40%), Exp4 (+10-30%), Exp5 (+10-20%)
cumulative_parameter_effects.mechanism: Sequential survival improvements (mortality reduction → drought tolerance → storage buffering → recruitment → seed input) create cumulative biomass recovery

storage_cushion_ecosystem_optimization.description: Adding alloc_storage_cushion_9 = 1.40 (Exp3) produces the largest improvement in MODIS LAI/GPP match while maintaining biomass gains
storage_cushion_ecosystem_optimization.mechanism: Higher storage cushion provides better C buffering leading to more stable biomass and more realistic LAI/GPP that better matches observations

seed_supplement_overshoot_effect.description: Seed supplement parameter (recruit_seed_supplement_9 = 0.045) causes LAI and GPP overshoot, degrading MODIS match
seed_supplement_overshoot_effect.mechanism: Too much external seed input leads to excessive recruitment, creating overly high LAI/GPP that overshoots MODIS observations by 21-24%

optimal_parameter_subset_identification.description: Exp3 or Exp4 (3-4 parameters) achieve optimal performance: top MODIS match + excellent PFT#9 biomass, while Exp5 (5 parameters) overshoots
optimal_parameter_subset_identification.mechanism: Recruitment parameters beyond seed decay rate cause excessive population recovery that overshoots realistic ecosystem function

nrmse_calculation_error.description: NRMSE composite metric was incorrectly calculated as arithmetic mean instead of root mean square
nrmse_calculation_error.mechanism: Proper formula is sqrt(mean(NRMSE²)) not mean(NRMSE) - RMS preserves quadratic penalty for large errors

fates_2d_parameter_structure.description: FATES uses 2D arrays for stoichiometry parameters with organ×PFT dimensions, not separate 1D parameters
fates_2d_parameter_structure.mechanism: Parameters like fates_stoich_nitr have dimensions (fates_plant_organs=4, fates_pft=12) where organs are 1=leaf, 2=fineroot, 3=sapwood, 4=storage

validation_range_method.description: Model validation uses ±20% of observed mean rather than standard deviation based ranges
validation_range_method.mechanism: VALID_LOW/VALID_HIGH boundaries set as 0.8 and 1.2 times observed mean values

morris_missing_critical_parameters.description: Critical parameter fates_turnover_fnrt was NOT included in Morris 138-parameter ensemble, causing systematic bias across all 4329 simulations
morris_missing_critical_parameters.mechanism: All simulations used same turnover rate (1.0 year for PFT#10) which is 5× too fast compared to literature (>5 years for Arctic fine roots). Morris optimization could not discover this bottleneck

morris_parameter_bounds_constraint.description: Case #2678 has 41 out of 138 parameters (29.7%) at their Morris ensemble bounds, indicating optimal values lie outside the Morris search space
morris_parameter_bounds_constraint.mechanism: Morris optimization pushed parameters toward bounds when those directions improved objective function but was constrained by search space limits

pft10_p_uptake_maxed_out.description: Both P uptake parameters for PFT#10 (vmax_p_10 and vmax_ptase_10) are at their UPPER Morris bounds, explaining severe P starvation
pft10_p_uptake_maxed_out.mechanism: Morris tried to maximize P uptake capacity but reached upper bounds of search space while P uptake remains 100,000x too low relative to demand

storage_cushion_seasonal_constraint.description: Morris minimized storage cushion (0.686) because it optimized summer biomass only, missing winter survival and spring regrowth constraints
storage_cushion_seasonal_constraint.mechanism: Morris objective function matched July 2016 biomass but couldn't see that PFT#10 drops leaves to zero in winter and must regrow entire canopy from storage

p_starvation_adaptation_strategy.description: PFT#10 exhibits P-starvation adaptation: maximizing N in leaves and P in roots while minimizing P in leaves
p_starvation_adaptation_strategy.mechanism: Under severe P limitation, plants prioritize scarce P for root P acquisition while maintaining high leaf N for photosynthesis and minimizing leaf P to conserve resources

eca_competitive_exclusion.description: PFT#9 obtains 2× more P than PFT#10 due to higher capacitance under ECA competition
eca_competitive_exclusion.mechanism: Under Equilibrium Chemistry Approximation, nutrient uptake emerges from simultaneous competition based on plant capacitance (fine-root biomass × vmax_p × root distribution). PFT#9 has higher capacitance due to more fineroot biomass

vmax_p_dominance_over_vmax_ptase.description: vmax_p changes cause allocation paradox while vmax_ptase changes cause only minor effects
vmax_p_dominance_over_vmax_ptase.mechanism: vmax_p directly affects P uptake and triggers PID allocation response, while vmax_ptase affects P release from organic matter without triggering same allocation response

morris_missing_eca_capacitance_parameter.description: Morris sampling is missing critical parameters that directly control ECA capacitance, the fundamental mechanism determining competitive nutrient uptake
morris_missing_eca_capacitance_parameter.mechanism: Capacitance = fine-root biomass × vmax_p × root distribution. Missing parameters (turnover, PID gains, root distribution) directly affect capacitance but were never optimized

pid_integral_control_disabled.description: PID integral control is disabled (ki=0) for ALL PFTs, meaning the controller is actually just a PD controller
pid_integral_control_disabled.mechanism: Without integral term, PID cannot eliminate persistent steady-state errors. For chronic nutrient limitation, integral term is essential to eliminate accumulated error over time

root_distribution_spatial_mismatch.description: PFT#10 has different root distribution parameters (a=11.0, b=2.0) compared to PFT#7/9 (a=7.0, b=1.5), potentially creating spatial mismatch with soil P pools
root_distribution_spatial_mismatch.mechanism: ECA competition occurs layer-by-layer in soil. If PFT#10 distribution poorly overlaps with soil P pools, it has disadvantage even with good total biomass

turnover_undermines_allocation_response.description: Fixed high turnover rates (1.0 yr for roots) undermine PID allocation responses by causing roots to die before accumulating competitive biomass
turnover_undermines_allocation_response.mechanism: Even when PID allocates more C to roots, high turnover (1.0 yr = roots last only 1 year) prevents buildup of steady-state biomass needed for competitive capacitance

arctic_root_distribution_contradiction.description: FATES default root distribution parameters for Arctic PFTs are contradictory to field observations - PFT#10 (graminoids) have most surface-concentrated roots in model but should be deepest rooted
arctic_root_distribution_contradiction.mechanism: Current parameters: PFT#10 (a=11.0, b=2.0) creates fastest exponential decay with depth, making graminoids most surface-concentrated. Field studies show Arctic sedges/grasses extend roots to permafrost boundary while evergreen shrubs concentrate in organic layer only

eca_spatial_mismatch_hypothesis.description: ECA nutrient competition occurs layer-by-layer, so spatial mismatch between root distribution and soil P profile could explain PFT#10 underperformance at Kougarok
eca_spatial_mismatch_hypothesis.mechanism: If soil P is concentrated at depth but PFT#10 roots are surface-concentrated due to wrong parameters, PFT#9 with deeper distribution gains competitive advantage through better overlap with P pools in each layer

unified_root_profile_control.description: FATES fnrt_prof parameters control ALL belowground biomass distribution, not just fine roots - includes coarse roots, litter inputs, respiration, and nutrient uptake capacity
unified_root_profile_control.mechanism: Single rootfrac_scr array calculated from fnrt_prof_a and fnrt_prof_b is used across multiple modules for fine root litter, coarse root litter, root respiration, fine root carbon density (for ECA), and water uptake weighting

graminoid_subsurface_root_peaks.description: 83.3% (5/6) graminoid cores show subsurface biomass peaks at 10-20 cm depth, with mean peak at 11.9 cm compared to surface peaks for all shrub species
graminoid_subsurface_root_peaks.mechanism: Active layer (10-20 cm) provides nutrient-rich mineral soil protected from surface freeze-thaw, allowing access to newly thawed nitrogen and phosphorus with reduced microbial competition

exponential_formula_mathematical_incompa.description: FATES 2-parameter exponential formula is mathematically incapable of representing subsurface biomass peaks due to monotonic decrease constraint
exponential_formula_mathematical_incompa.mechanism: Both exponential terms have negative derivatives (df/dz = -a·exp(-a·z) - b·exp(-b·z) < 0), meaning maximum is always at surface (z=0) by mathematical definition

backwards_parameter_ranking_confirmed.description: Current FATES defaults make graminoids most surface-concentrated (a=11.0, b=2.0) when field data shows they should be deepest rooted (mean depth 21.4 cm vs 7.7-10.2 cm for shrubs)
backwards_parameter_ranking_confirmed.mechanism: Higher a,b values create faster exponential decay resulting in more surface roots, while observed graminoid biology requires deeper, more uniform distribution

elm_layer_aggregation_smoothing_effect.description: ELM 15-layer mapping with depth-weighted averaging smooths subsurface peaks, creating artificial 'good fits' with exponential formulas that don't reflect true biology
elm_layer_aggregation_smoothing_effect.mechanism: Spatial aggregation across varying ELM layer thickness smears subsurface peaks (15-20 cm) across multiple layers, making exponential approximation appear acceptable despite wrong parameters

graminoid_deep_rooting_strategy.description: Graminoids show specialized rooting strategy with peak biomass at 10-20 cm depth and extensions to permafrost boundary (50-100 cm according to literature)
graminoid_deep_rooting_strategy.mechanism: Three-layer strategy: thin surface roots (0-10 cm), peak biomass in active layer (10-20 cm) for nutrient access, and sparse deep roots (20+ cm) extending toward permafrost for deep nutrient pools

soil_phosphorus_chemistry_bottleneck.description: ELM soil order parameters create P trap where 98.9% of soil P (202 g P m⁻³) is locked in mineral-adsorbed pool while only 0.00002% is plant-available (4×10⁻⁵ g P m⁻³)
soil_phosphorus_chemistry_bottleneck.mechanism: Desorption rate is 23× slower than adsorption rate for Gelisols (r_desorp=0.00022 vs r_adsorp=0.005), creating equilibrium heavily favoring adsorbed state despite abundant total P

morris_optimization_parameter_domain_lim.description: Morris ensemble varied 138 FATES plant parameters but never varied ELM soil chemistry parameters that control P availability
morris_optimization_parameter_domain_lim.mechanism: Soil chemistry parameters are in separate file (CNP_parameters_c180312.nc) indexed by soil order, not PFT, so were fixed throughout all 4170 Morris simulations

phosphorus_desorption_supply_demand_imba.description: Plant P demand (6×10⁻³ g P m⁻³ day⁻¹) exceeds desorption supply (1.5×10⁻³ g P m⁻³ day⁻¹) by 4×, causing LABILEP depletion
phosphorus_desorption_supply_demand_imba.mechanism: Desorption can't keep up with plant uptake despite large SECONDP pool, resulting in mass-action limitation where uptake becomes proportional to near-zero LABILEP concentration

cross_pft_sensitivity_pervasive.description: Morris analysis shows 20-40% of top-10 parameter rankings come from OTHER PFTs, indicating strong cross-PFT interactions
cross_pft_sensitivity_pervasive.mechanism: PFT parameters affect other PFTs through light competition and nutrient depletion

root_distribution_backwards_arctic.description: Current root distribution parameters may be backwards for Arctic tundra - graminoids have shallowest roots when they should be deepest
root_distribution_backwards_arctic.mechanism: Graminoids (PFT#10) have highest a,b parameters giving shallowest roots (mean depth 0.31 m), but field observations show graminoids should be deepest to permafrost, evergreens shallowest

edge_parameters_appear_insensitive.description: Parameters at Morris bounds show low sensitivity because they can't vary in one direction, making them appear unimportant when they may actually be constrained
edge_parameters_appear_insensitive.mechanism: 41/138 parameters (29.7%) were at Morris bounds for Case #2678. Parameters at bounds show low |μ| because they can't vary in one direction

eca_capacitance_formula.description: ECA capacitance is determined by the formula: Capacitance = vmax_p × root_biomass × distribution
eca_capacitance_formula.mechanism: Nutrient uptake capacity depends on uptake rate per root (vmax_p), total root biomass, and spatial distribution overlap with nutrient pools

integral_pid_term_disabled.description: PID integral term is currently OFF (ki=0) when chronic nutrient limitation may require allocation memory
integral_pid_term_disabled.mechanism: Integral term eliminates persistent C:nutrient errors and provides memory of chronic nutrient limitation, but currently fixed at 0

arctic_pft_parameter_expansion.description: Expanded Morris ensemble from 138 to 162 parameters by adding 24 new parameters targeting Arctic PFTs #7, #9, and #10
arctic_pft_parameter_expansion.mechanism: Added turnover rates, root distribution, PID control, and nutrient storage parameters for specific Arctic plant functional types to capture previously uncharacterized mechanisms

pft_netcdf_indexing.description: PFT indices in NetCDF files are 0-based, requiring mapping from PFT numbers to array indices
pft_netcdf_indexing.mechanism: NetCDF arrays use 0-based indexing while PFT numbers are 1-based, requiring translation (PFT#7→index 6, PFT#9→index 8, PFT#10→index 9)

p_uptake_bottleneck_identified.description: P uptake parameters (vmax_p and vmax_ptase) were maxed out at Morris bounds in best-performing case, with P uptake/demand ratio ≈ 0.000005
p_uptake_bottleneck_identified.mechanism: P starvation prevents root growth even with high allocation, creating fundamental growth bottleneck

root_distribution_backwards.description: Current default root distribution parameters are backwards compared to field observations - graminoids have deepest roots (to permafrost) but model shows shallowest
root_distribution_backwards.mechanism: Field calibration from 56 cores shows PFT#10 (graminoid) has deepest roots (mean depth 0.31m), contradicting model defaults

morris_bounds_too_narrow.description: Original Morris bounds were 345-510% too narrow for root distribution parameters compared to field-calibrated values
morris_bounds_too_narrow.mechanism: Field-calibrated values: PFT#7 b=10.355 and PFT#9 b=18.289 exceed upper bound of 3.0 by 345% and 510% respectively

opposite_competition_strategies.description: Best-performing cases use opposite plant-microbe competition strategies with different microbial biomass levels
opposite_competition_strategies.mechanism: Case #2678: Low microb_bio_7 (140), high microb_bio_10 (340). Case #845: High microb_bio_7 (380), low microb_bio_10 (180)

fates_missing_vegetative_reproduction.description: FATES has no vegetative reproduction pathway for graminoids - all reproduction flows through seed pool only
fates_missing_vegetative_reproduction.mechanism: Code verification shows only seed-based reproduction pathway, while real Arctic graminoids reproduce 60-90% via vegetative propagation

hydraulic_mortality_drought_sensitivity.description: Case 2678 with 2× r_desorp revealed massive vegetation collapse during 1963-1968 Alaska drought. PFT#7 (evergreen shrub) experienced 98% mortality due to HYDRAULIC FAILURE, not carbon starvation.
hydraulic_mortality_drought_sensitivity.mechanism: During drought, btran dropped to essentially zero, triggering massive hydraulic mortality. Hydraulic mortality was 426 g C/m²/yr while C starvation was only 0.03 g C/m²/yr.

morris_ensemble_162_parameters_successfu.description: Successfully generated and verified Morris ensemble with 162 parameters (138 original + 24 new) including 4890 parameter sets with correct dimensions and parameter ordering.
morris_ensemble_162_parameters_successfu.mechanism: Morris method with 30 trajectories × 163 samples per trajectory, using 8 grid levels and seed 123. All parameter files verified with 100% match rate across 16,200 parameter checks.

litter_p_accumulation_not_loss.description: P does not leave the system during vegetation collapse - it accumulates in litter pools instead
litter_p_accumulation_not_loss.mechanism: Dead vegetation produces massive litter input while drought suppresses decomposition through low w_scalar, causing P to be trapped in litter rather than cycling

hydraulic_mortality_dominates_drought_re.description: Hydraulic failure mortality, not carbon starvation, was the primary cause of PFT7 death during 1963-1968 drought
hydraulic_mortality_dominates_drought_re.mechanism: Soil moisture crashed causing btran to drop below hf_sm_threshold, triggering hydraulic mortality that was 14,000x higher than carbon starvation mortality

pft_differential_drought_survival.description: Different PFTs have vastly different drought survival - PFT7 (evergreen shrub) died while PFT9 (deciduous) and PFT10 (graminoid) survived
pft_differential_drought_survival.mechanism: PFT7 had 98% mortality by 1970 while PFT9 survived and PFT10 thrived, suggesting different drought tolerance parameters across PFTs

drought_decomposition_coupling.description: Drought suppresses litter decomposition through w_scalar effects, creating a feedback that traps nutrients in litter
drought_decomposition_coupling.mechanism: Low soil moisture reduces w_scalar in decomp_k calculation, slowing litter breakdown while vegetation mortality increases litter input

chronic_nutrient_limitation_reduces_resi.description: Plants were getting less than 1% of their nutrient demand, making them vulnerable to additional stressors
chronic_nutrient_limitation_reduces_resi.mechanism: P uptake/demand ratios dropped from 23% in ADSP to 0.08% in TRANS, creating chronic stress that reduced ability to cope with drought
